Although CHERI-based systems may initially involve higher learning and adoption costs, these can be offset by improved security outcomes and reduced lifecycle risk.

The CRA introduces differentiated conformity assessment paths depending on product risk. While some lower-risk products may qualify for self-assessment, higher-risk categories will require independent third-party assessment.

This has important implications for supply chains. Vendors will increasingly need to demonstrate that their components — including hardware, firmware, and software libraries — support compliance. As a result, pressure to adopt more robust security foundations is likely to cascade down to suppliers and technology partners.
Standards aligned with CRA requirements are already emerging, and future revisions of the regulation may raise the bar further — potentially including explicit expectations around memory safety.
Although full enforcement is still over a year away, time is running out! The CRA is already shaping procurement decisions, product roadmaps, and architectural choices.
Those that act early will be better positioned not only to meet compliance deadlines, but to compete in a market where security is increasingly a differentiator rather than a checkbox.

The Cyber Resilience Act signals a clear change in direction for product security. This will not only have an impact in Europe, but also in the rest of the World as manufacturers usually design products that are sold globally and need to fit the most stringent requirements. By making cybersecurity a legal requirement at the point of design, it encourages a move away from reactive fixes and towards fundamentally safer systems.

For organisations willing to invest in secure-by-design architectures such as CHERI, the CRA is not just a compliance challenge — it is an opportunity to build more resilient products, reduce long-term risk, and establish trust in an increasingly security-conscious market.
That is why lowRISC's announcement that OpenTitan Earl Grey 2 will support CHERI is important.

OpenTitan is an open source hardware Root of Trust platform designed to protect some of the most sensitive parts of a system. The Earl Grey 2 version will add CHERI support through a CHERIoT configuration of the Ibex processor, alongside post-quantum cryptography and other security improvements.
For developers and organisations, this means another practical route to using CHERI in real hardware.

CHERI helps prevent memory safety vulnerabilities and provides fine-grained software compartmentalisation enforced by the processor. Instead of relying entirely on software behaving correctly, hardware places stronger limits on what code is allowed to access.

This matters when the code handles keys, firmware, secure boot, device identity or other security-critical functions. CHERI can isolate each of those processes so that a vulnerability in one of them would not give an attacker access to anything else.

Earl Grey 2 will keep CHERI optional, allowing existing users to continue using legacy ePMP-based protection while giving new projects the opportunity to design with stronger hardware-enforced protections from the outset.
This new version of OpenTitan demonstrates how CHERI can bring an additional layer of security to real systems.

As AI makes it easier to discover, understand and potentially exploit software vulnerabilities at scale, reducing the impact of those vulnerabilities becomes increasingly important. Memory safety, compartmentalisation, Root of Trust and post-quantum security are becoming part of the same wider challenge. We need to build systems that integrate more of those security by design technologies to protect devices preventively as both threats and attackers' capabilities evolve.

The QEMU emulator is critical for systems research and development: it makes it possible to quickly prototype, debug and analyse architectural extensions and OS implementations without the need for dedicated hardware implementations in FPGA or silicon.
QEMU monitoring features, such as instruction-level tracing and GDB integration are particularly important to make system software development easier.

It is important to remember that QEMU is not a system simulator (such as gem5 https://www.gem5.org) and it does not attempt to be cycle-accurate. Instead, it is a functionally accurate emulation of the target platform. This is very useful for systems validation and development, but it is not representative of CHERI systems' performance.

The QEMU emulator maintains a central role in the CHERI software ecosystem. Historically, CHERI support in QEMU dates back to the initial MIPS CHERI prototypes, with both 128-bit compressed and 256-bit uncompressed capabilities, developed at the University of Cambridge and SRI.

The convergence of multiple QEMU CHERI patches into a single reference implementation has been almost a year-long process throughout 2025 that involved contributors from multiple organisations, including the University of Cambridge, Capabilities Limited, Codasip and Google.

As of January 2026, we are excited to announce that the CHERI Alliance hosts a reference QEMU implementation that supports multiple modern CHERI platforms based on Arm and RISC-V. These include the Arm Morello platform, the CHERI RISC-V standard draft 0.9.3 and the University of Cambridge RISC-V ISA v9.
The CHERI Alliance reference implementation is an important milestone for future development and integration of CHERI support in QEMU.

Downstream users can now rely on a common implementation and a central repository for tracking issues and submitting CHERI-related patches. This effort is also contributing to the expansion of the CHERI Alliance CI infrastructure, with the goal of both providing stable QEMU images to test third-party software and validating QEMU itself.

The QEMU Working Group has set out three major goals for 2026: integrate CHERI patches on more modern QEMU versions, continue work to support the latest and upcoming iterations of the CHERI RISC-V standard, and improve the QEMU CI infrastructure.

The current CHERI patches are maintained on top of a relatively old QEMU version v7.0.0. This is becoming a substantial limitation for CHERI development, as this version lacks support for some important RISC-V extensions. The reference implementation is expected to reach QEMU v8 in the coming months.

As the CHERI RISC-V standard is finalised, the goal of the QEMU Working Group is committed to facilitate support and refinement for the standard CHERI RISC-V platforms, such as the Codasip X730 application core on the Codasip Prime platform.

Finally, the Working Group is refining the approach for testing and validation of the reference QEMU CHERI. In particular, The Capable Hub is contributing to establish a robust CI infrastructure for QEMU and the wider CHERI Alliance software ecosystem.

We expect 2026 to be an exciting year for the CHERI Alliance and the CHERI QEMU community as a whole. With no shortage of work in sight, we would like to encourage members of the Alliance and any other organisation interested in CHERI to check out the latest developments at https://github.com/CHERI-Alliance/qemu and join the monthly QEMU WG meetings by registering to the wg-qemu mailing list https://lists.cheri-alliance.org.
We are proud to see that the CHERI Alliance is highlighted in this report, even though the Alliance was only recently formed.

A groundbreaking paper from the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory (DSTL) – Biting the CHERI bullet: Blockers, Enablers and Security Implications of CHERI in Defence – sheds light on the transformative potential of CHERI (Capability Hardware Enhanced RISC Instructions) technology, offering a beacon of hope for enhancing cyber resilience. The paper described:

This insightful study not only identifies the challenges faced during the adoption of CHERI but also helps us chart a clear roadmap for future improvements, and acceleration of the adoption of the technology by the industry:

The positive contributions of this paper are manifold. By meticulously evaluating CHERI through a 12-month assessment involving 15 teams from industry and academia, the DSTL paper provides a comprehensive understanding of the technology's strengths and areas for improvement. It highlights the significant strides made in memory safety, the effectiveness of CHERI-enabled tools, and the improved code quality and security that CHERI brings to the table.

Moreover, the paper's findings have already sparked significant interest and action within the tech community. Codasip, a leading player in the field, has written a compelling blog post discussing the recent advances in CHERI, emphasizing progress in stability, maturity, and accessibility. This growing momentum underscores the importance of the DSTL paper and its potential to drive widespread adoption of CHERI.

As we delve deeper into the key findings and define a roadmap from the ideas extracted from the DSTL paper, we invite you to join us on this journey towards a more secure and resilient digital world. Together, we can unlock the full potential of CHERI technology and pave the way for a safer future.

One of the primary challenges identified by DSTL as inhibiting the smooth adoption of CHERI is tool chain instability and the lack of maturity at the time of the study. Teams struggled with the absence of familiar utilities, such as Integrated Development Environments (IDEs) and functional debuggers, and often had to resort to less efficient development methods, which complicated the development process. Performance of the early prototypes was also highlighted as a negative point. These topics have already been addressed in the Codasip paper and indeed a huge amount of work has already been done to provide stable tools and good development platforms. For example, the mention of a lack of temporal safety is now inaccurate: all specifications and actual implementations include it.

That doesn't mean that everything is in place yet! I will highlight that the work on tools and software continues and the CHERI Alliance is taking a proactive approach in getting all contributors to collaborate as part of its working groups. This is already leading to faster progress on major operating systems (Linux, FreeRTOS, Zephyr, seL4) as more people and companies join the effort. We need to continue and extend this collaboration to make sure that the Alliance helps reduce duplication of effort and therefore improves the efficiency of this porting activity.

Since the DSTL teams were new to CHERI, they found the learning curve difficult, because of inaccurate or missing documentation, lack of guidance, and a shortage of comprehensive examples. Again, although much progress has been made since then and it is still an area that needs to improve: there is no practical reason why using CHERI should be difficult.

Furthermore, amongst the millions of software developers worldwide, there is a broad variety of expertise, especially about the lowest levels of memory management, even more as the focus of education has shifted to high-level languages like Python. This lack of background knowledge might make memory-safety issues more difficult to understand.

This stimulates us to focus our energy on this "developer enablement", where the CHERI Alliance would help get easier access to available documentation, but also create new content targeted towards different audiences. This is part of our mission to accelerate adoption of CHERI.

The paper also highlights that technical debt in existing software was a critical issue, with teams encountering problems related to pointer size assumptions, new signal handling mechanisms, and the need to refactor legacy code to be handled by the latest tool versions. These challenges necessitated careful consideration and additional effort to ensure compatibility and stability. Even though some teams found the process of porting code to CHERI to be relatively straightforward, requiring minimal changes to their existing codebase, we definitely need to develop "CHERI adaption skills" as it will encourage more teams to adopt CHERI and reduce the effort and resources required for migration.

Since one of the key values of CHERI resides in the ability to reuse existing software, it is crucial to train developers to understand how to best adapt and optimise code to run on CHERI systems. A lot of experience has been accumulated by the teams working on CHERI for the past years (and some for more than a decade!), and we need to find the best ways to transfer this knowledge to the industry. At the moment, the Alliance is solving this by facilitating collaboration between experienced CHERI developers and new ones within the working groups and the various networking opportunities, but we indeed need to find more scalable ways to train the teams that need to update thousands (or even millions) of different products.

Despite these challenges, the DSTL paper also identifies several enablers that can facilitate the adoption and success of CHERI technology. One of the most significant enablers is the effectiveness of CHERI-enabled compilers and debuggers, which are notably more adept at detecting memory safety issues. These tools can significantly enhance the security and reliability of software developed for CHERI. Obviously, as this is the key benefit of CHERI, teams reported improved code quality and security as a result of adopting CHERI, thanks to its fine-grained memory protection capabilities.

As part of its mission to popularise CHERI, the CHERI Alliance should definitely continue focusing on communicating the benefits of the technology, to all concerned audiences. The marketing working group relies on the help and resources of the members of the Alliance, and will need to continue this evangelisation effort, while also adapting the message to different audiences. Again, a lot of energy needs to be spent there, but the benefit of a growing collaborative community is that its efforts get multiplied by the number of participating members... So we can only continue to encourage all motivated parties to join our community!

The DSTL paper provides valuable insights into the adoption of CHERI technology. By addressing the identified technical and knowledge blockers and highlighting the benefits of the technology, the CHERI Alliance can pave the way for wider adoption and improved security in hardware foundations.

This paper stimulates us to further advance our initiatives and broaden the integration of "security by design" into products across all industry segments. The CHERI Alliance has only just started its mission of accelerating CHERI adoption, and we count on you to help us achieve this goal!
Interview with Ron Black, CEO of Codasip

Codasip is a founding member of the CHERI Alliance and one of the most active industrial players in the CHERI ecosystem. From the outset, Codasip has played an active role in CHERI Alliance activities—taking part in technical discussions, leading some working groups, contributing open-source software, supporting standardisation efforts, and helping bridge the gap between the CHERI research community and commercial deployment. Alongside this work, the company has invested in making CHERI tangible for the ecosystem, through commercially available CHERI‐RISC‐V IP and development platforms that allow partners to experiment, prototype, and build products.

"There has been interest from security experts in CHERI since its conception over a decade ago. Now, after the formation of the CHERI Alliance for standardisation and promotion, we have begun to see true market pull. Consequently, Codasip invested early to create commercially available CHERI-RISC-V processors with all the required base software, such as the operating systems, compilers, and debuggers, etc. Interest has increased further with our launch of these products, especially after we began offering our Codasip Prime FPGA development kit that allows hardware and software engineers to start their development with production level IP and software."

"Simple reason really – many customers, especially in the defence and critical infrastructure segments, prefer to engage with us in physical products, so after several made the request, we just did what they asked."
"Two actually. Application Software, but that won't occur until the silicon and base software is completed. And standardization and regulation to ensure the ecosystem is aligned."

"We see defence as being the first commercial adopter, which is not surprising given that DARPA funded the early research and proof of the technology. Mid-term it is a broad set of applications that fall into "Critical National Infrastructure or CNI" category. And clearly with all the gray-zone conflicts and state-sponsored cyberattacks, CNI is the real risk to every nation. The CHERI "pump" is being "primed", and really all companies in all industries that care about their customers should have a CHERI programme in our opinion."

"When speaking with non-technical people we frequently use the model of infectious disease, likening CHERI to a "cyber vaccine" for memory safety "cyber viruses." With the exponential increase in CVEs, cyberattacks have gone from endemic to an epidemic, and are only going to get worse with AI.

As the primary goal of government is to protect its people, and government provides free vaccines during an epidemic to protect its citizens, it only makes sense that government takes a leadership role in ensuring cyber protection. Certainly the defence industry, which is funded by the government, sees that. It is not clear if governments are taking enough action, however, in CNI. In our opinion, more is needed now, before there is a major issue. I would really hate to be a government that did nothing to protect its citizens, when the "cyber vaccine" was already proven and ready for mass production. And the EU has now taken the step with its Cyber Resilience Act, or CRA, to ensure accountability by end system producers.
But whilst the product manufacturers are liable, they are dependent on the supply chain, where these requirements now need to be implemented."

"We recently announced a sale of the low-end of our product line, which is not CHERI enabled. The acquirer also took a broad license to StudioTM, our processor design EDA tool. We can still use these processors in physical products (FPGAs and chips), and will CHERI enable them to do so, but we will not be focusing on licensing non-CHERI products, and most of our focus is now on mid-range and high-performance out-of-order processors where there is more demand and value."
"A successful semiconductor company leading the way in resilient by design SoC solutions."

Building on its existing work with CHERI, Wind River was recently awarded a contract as part of a strategic initiative led by Innovate UK and the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology to support the wider adoption of CHERI technology. As part of this effort, they will be working to port and extend the VxWorks Real-Time Operating System (RTOS) and Wind River Helix Virtualization Platform (Helix Platform) to leverage the CHERI architecture on RISC-V.

The addition of Wind River is a significant boost to our mission to accelerate CHERI adoption. By combining proven, industry-grade software with CHERI's hardware-enforced protections, we move closer to reducing entire classes of memory safety vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure and intelligent edge devices.
We look forward to working with Wind River as part of the Alliance.

The CHERI Alliance brings together industry, research, government, and open-source communities to accelerate the adoption of CHERI technology. As a neutral international non-profit organisation based in Cambridge, it helps connect the people, projects, and organisations building CHERI into real-world products and platforms.
New technologies need more than technical innovation. They need a community, a shared direction, and a voice.

The Alliance serves as a collective voice for the CHERI ecosystem, helping communicate the benefits of memory-safe computing to industry, governments, standards bodies, researchers, and potential adopters.
The Alliance also helps create demand for CHERI by bringing together technology developers, suppliers, users, and adopters around a shared vision for more secure computing.

CHERI's progress depends on collaboration across many communities. Researchers, implementers, product teams, government programmes, standards bodies, and open-source contributors all have different roles to play. The Alliance provides a neutral forum where those communities can align around practical adoption while retaining ownership of their own projects and priorities.

Members contribute expertise and requirements, share work where collaboration is useful, and learn from organisations solving related problems. Public resources and open projects also allow participation beyond formal membership.
The Alliance accelerates CHERI adoption by:

The Alliance supports collaboration, technical exchange, education, and adoption across the CHERI ecosystem. Product vendors, standards bodies, governments, and research organisations continue to own their own technologies, priorities, and decisions.
The Alliance works closely with partners across the ecosystem, including the CHERI Research Centre and The Capable Hub. Learn more about how we accelerate CHERI together.

The CHERI Alliance is an independent, non-profit organisation, organised as a UK Community Interest Company (CIC). This means we are subject to the same accounting and reporting obligations as other companies, while also being regulated to ensure that our activities are carried out for the benefit of the wider community. In our case, the mission is to accelerate CHERI adoption by the industry. This structure also ensures that the Alliance cannot be acquired in the way a conventional company can.

From 2022 until March 2025, Digital Catapult managed and delivered the DSbD Technology Access Programme (TAP), funded by UKRI and in collaboration with the University of Cambridge, ARM and lowRISC.

The programme accelerated awareness and advancement of the CHERI (Capability Hardware Enhanced RISC Instructions) framework, convening businesses across multiple sectors to experiment with the Morello and Sonata boards. In addition to providing participants with access to hardware, Digital Catapult also provided technical support and project guidance.

Across the delivery of 6 cohorts, made up of 51 different companies from across the UK, TAP helped validate the security benefits of CHERI, demonstrating its ability to detect and prevent memory vulnerabilities, as well as the additional trust and performance available from the adoption of compartmentalisation models. TAP demonstrated how CHERI can be used for enhancing application security and reducing attack surfaces in their own and/or third-party code. Cohort companies validated that CHERI would have identified known issues much more quickly and helped mitigate vulnerabilities before product deployment, and were also able to identify clear business opportunities for using CHERI in new and existing products.

In addition, Digital Catapult built a Remote Lab, allowing companies to access a virtual platform hosted on Morello for CI/CD with CheriBSD. More information on this can be found here: https://github.com/dc-dsbd

CheriBSD extends FreeBSD to implement memory protection and software compartmentalization features supported by the CHERI instruction-set extensions. CheriBSD is a research operating system with a stable baseline implementation into which various new research features have been, or are currently being, merged.

A debug trap enters debug mode. This places the core under the control of the debug unit (which contains some ROM and RAM).
When in debug mode, CHERI checks are omitted, so code in the debug unit can access all of memory.
This mode is not controllable by software executing on the core, only by an external debugger (typically connected via JTAG).

SoCs that integrated this core are expected to fuse off the debug unit for production deployments, completely disabling this functionality. Alternatively, custom debug ROM code may also restrict the behaviour of the debug mode.

The hardware revoker is integrated with the load-store unit. It scans all of revokable memory and clears tags on capabilities that have been marked as revoked. This does not require a capability to authorise it, but its behaviour is strictly limited. It can clear tags, but not otherwise manipulate capabilities or values. This is part of the temporal safety mechanism and defines the abstract machine. Software can restrict the range over which the revoker runs and can instruct it to begin, but cannot make it do anything other than clear tags on capabilities that point to deallocated objects within that range.

The CHERIoT ISA does not include any hybrid modes or privilege levels that would require flows for setting tags on capabilities owned by less-privileged parts of the system. The system boots with three root capabilities (read+execute, read+write, sealing) and all capabilities in the system are derived from this.
The VeriCHERI work conforms that all operations implemented by the core respect the capability monotonicity properties: tags can be cleared, but not set.

Note that this property is specific to the core. A hypothetical implementation could expose the backing store for tags on the memory bus. SoCs using this core that are requesting certification should justify such a decision and describe appropriate safeguards.
The core does not support SMP configurations. It does support integration with DMA units that do not write tags.

The core is designed to be used both in new systems and those with existing 32-bit bus architectures with minimal changes. As such, it supports connecting to the memory in two ways. If the design has flexibility (and area) for a 65-bit memory interface, then capabilities are loaded and stored from the core in a single 65-bit transaction, carrying the tag and the data. Capability loads and stores are always aligned and so cannot cover part of a tagged value.

For incremental adoption, the memory bus can also be configured in 33-bit (typically using user-defined metadata bits on an existing bus design to carry the extra bit). This requires two bus transactions to load or store a capability.
In 65-bit mode, stores from the core carry the tag bit and so every capability store is atomic.

In 33-bit mode, capability stores are two 33-bit stores, which each carry the tag. When a normal 32-bit store is issued, it will clear the tag bit for that 33-bit word in memory. When the core loads a capability, it will issue two 33-bit loads and then AND together the resulting tag bits to give the architectural tag bit.

Consider two adjacent memory locations A and B. The core first does a store of a capability spanning both. The tag bits in both will be set. It then does a store of a 32-bit word (narrower stores use byte enables on a 32-bit bus transaction) over A, which clears A's tag bit. When the core does a load-capability at this location, it sees 01 as the pair of tag bits. ANDing these together gives 0: the result is untagged.
Integrators who use the core with DMA in 33-bit mode must take some care, and certifying a product with such a mode raises some additional questions, depending on the integration:
If DMA can write capabilities then the memory controller must ensure that tag-setting stores from two bus masters are not interleaved and DV must ensure that this is the case.

If DMA cannot store capabilities, interleaving is normally not a problem: a 33-bit store from the CPU that sets a tag interleaved with a 32-bit store from DMA that clears a tag will result in one tag bit being zeroed. However, for area optimisation, an implementation may use a 33-bit bus but still store a single tag bit per 64-bit word. In a situation with no DMA, this is fine: the core will always set tags by writing two tag-setting values back to back. With DMA, the memory controller must ensure that the sequence of a tag-set store to A from the core, a tag-cleared store to A from DMA, and a tag-set store to B from the DMA results in a load of A having its tag bit cleared. DV results for certification of SoCs in this configuration should explicitly document that this has been tested.
CHERIoT temporal safety is implemented in two parts, extensively documented in two papers describing the CHERIoT platform:

Saar Amar, David Chisnall, Tony Chen, Nathaniel Filardo Wesley, Ben Laurie, Kunyan Liu, Robert Norton, Simon W. Moore, Yucong Tao, Robert N. M. Watson and Hongyan Xia. CHERIoT: Complete Memory Safety for Embedded Devices. proceedings of the 56th IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Microarchitecture, Association for Computing Machinery (2023).

Saar Amar, Tony Chen, David Chisnall, Nathaniel Wesley Filardo, Ben Laurie, Hugo Lefeuvre, Kunyan Liu, Simon W. Moore, Robert Norton-Wright, Margo Seltzer, Yucong Tao, Robert N. M. Watson and Hongyan Xia. CHERIoT RTOS: An OS for Fine-Grained Memory-Safe Compartments on Low-Cost Embedded Devices. Proceedings of the ACM SIGOPS 31st Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, Association for Computing Machinery (2025), 67–84.

Each granule (8 bytes in the CHERIoT Ibex implementation) of memory that may be used as a heap has a one bit revocation bit associated with it. When an object is freed, the memory allocator sets the revocation bits corresponding to all memory that forms part of the freed object.

The ISA mandates a load filter, which checks the base of capabilities loaded capabilities against the revocation bitmap. The monotonicity properties of CHERI bounds ensure that one of the following is true:
The capability length is zero (in which case the base may point to the address immediately after the end of an allocation), or
The base address is within the range of the original allocation.

The load filter therefore ensures that it is impossible to load a capability that points to memory that is marked as freed. The memory allocator must ensure that, on return from free, all registers are either zeroed or spilled and reloaded. This happens automatically for other threads (context switching to another thread always involves spilling and restoring all registers).
This mechanism is enough to guarantee deterministic trapping on user-after-free bugs. It is not sufficient to allow deallocated memory to be reused.

The CHERIoT-Ibex also implements a revocation engine, which steals cycles from the load-store unit when not executing a load or store. This scans all memory and clears the tag on any capability that points to heap memory that has been marked as free (using the same check as the load filter). This, in combination with the load filter, guarantees that all memory that was freed at the start of a sweep is safe to reuse at the end. The allocator may then clear the revocation bits in such objects and reuse their memory.

These mechanism do, in theory, allow zero-length capabilities to the end of an object to survive revocation. This is not a security issue because zero-length capabilities convey no rights to access memory. The default CHERIoT allocator uses the revocation bit as a defence-in-depth protection for heap metadata and so a capability one past the end will always have its base refer to memory marked as freed and so, in normal operation, these zero-length capabilities cannot escape revocation.

Small connected devices often run many components in one address space: network stacks, parsers, drivers, third-party libraries, update code, and application logic. A fault in one can reach everything. Conventional process isolation may be unavailable or too heavy for the device.
CHERIoT is a CHERI-based hardware-software platform designed for this embedded environment.
These parts are designed together. CHERIoT is therefore more than a generic RISC-V core with capability instructions added.

Firmware is divided into compartments and libraries. The build description identifies components, dependencies, threads, entry points, stacks, and board configuration. The real-time operating system (RTOS) creates protected transitions and controls authority between compartments.

A network component can receive a capability for one packet and selected services without receiving authority for the complete firmware image. Capability bounds and permissions protect object access, while the compartment model limits the objects and services available to the component.
CHERIoT also provides mechanisms for temporal safety, helping prevent stale capabilities accessing storage after it has been reused.

Developers can begin without hardware using the formal-model simulator or implementation simulation. For physical development, supported targets include FPGA platforms such as Sonata and other boards listed by the project.

The ecosystem also includes commercial silicon and licensable processor designs. The CHERI product directory records the current platform landscape; suppliers retain responsibility for device, software development kit (SDK), and lifecycle information.

CHERIoT has a stable 1.0 architecture and RTOS line, released open-source implementations, development platforms, commercial silicon activity, and CHERI Enabled certification for the CHERIoT Ibex product. Individual repositories continue to evolve, so pin releases for reproducible product work.
The CHERIoT Programmer's Guide is the best starting point for architecture, compartments, memory management, drivers, auditing, and practical examples.

FPGA platforms provide a practical step between software simulation and production silicon. They let developers run CHERI processor and system designs on physical hardware, test software and peripherals, and modify the underlying hardware design without fabricating a chip.
Unlike a software simulator, an FPGA can implement the processor together with caches, memory, buses, interrupts and peripherals, allowing developers to test more of the complete system.
Usually not when you are getting started. Most developers can begin learning CHERI, porting software and investigating capability violations using simulation or QEMU.

An FPGA becomes useful when you need to test a processor or complete system design on physical hardware, measure performance, integrate peripherals, create demonstrations, or develop software before production silicon is available.
An FPGA is a chip that can be configured to contain a processor and other digital hardware. To run CHERI, you generally need a complete hardware and software environment, including:

Sonata provides an integrated development environment for CHERIoT software and physical peripherals. It is a good choice for developers who want to work with real hardware without building their own FPGA system.

CHERI processor designs can also run on supported commercial FPGA development boards. The Digilent Genesys 2 and AMD/Xilinx VCU118 have both been used extensively as FPGA platforms for CHERI-related processor and system development, and provide useful reference points for teams building or evaluating their own systems.

These platforms provide greater flexibility, particularly when you need more FPGA resources, memory or interfaces, but require more hardware-integration work than a purpose-built platform such as Sonata.
The processor, system design, board configuration and SDK must all be compatible. A bitstream built for one board cannot normally be used directly on another.
Application-class CHERI-RISC-V processors are larger, more complex designs, typically requiring more capable FPGA boards with greater logic, memory and system resources.

These platforms can support 64-bit CHERI-RISC-V systems suitable for operating-system and processor development. They are particularly useful when simulation such as QEMU is too abstract, but production silicon is not yet available or selected.

Processor-IP suppliers may provide FPGA images and SDKs for evaluating their CHERI-enabled processors. These can provide a supported route to product evaluation, although availability, licensing, supported peripherals and redistribution terms vary by supplier.

However, FPGA measurements do not directly represent final silicon: clock frequency, power consumption, chip area and memory performance will depend on the eventual implementation.

For reproducible development, record the RTL revision, FPGA tool version, synthesis settings, board configuration, bitstream, firmware and SDK used. FPGA build results can vary between tool versions, so the build environment is part of the platform configuration.

Developed by Arm in collaboration with the University of Cambridge and SRI International through the UK Digital Security by Design (DSbD) programme, Morello brings CHERI capabilities to an application-class processor and development board.
It provides developers with a complete environment for exploring CHERI on real high-performance hardware, including operating systems, toolchains and substantial applications.
Morello is one prototype implementation of CHERI, not CHERI itself. Other CHERI platforms, including CHERI-RISC-V and CHERIoT, use different architectures and software environments.
cheribuild is a common open-source route for building Morello LLVM, CheriBSD, disk images, and related tools from compatible source revisions.

Morello was designed for research, development and evaluation rather than as a mass-market production processor. For new commercial products, developers should consider current CHERI platforms and their availability, support and lifecycle.
The CHERI Alliance has Morello boards available for loan to organisations working on projects that can help advance CHERI development and adoption.
Boards are limited, so requests should explain clearly what you plan to do and why access to Morello hardware would be valuable.
Contact the CHERI Alliance to request a board ---
You can also find further information about the platform from Arm's Morello page.
A typical Morello project starts with a compatible software environment and known working example before moving on to your own software.
You should know whether the binaries you are working with are conventional, hybrid or pure capability, and keep the firmware, operating system, toolchain and ABI versions compatible.
For development, debugging and porting guidance, use the technical documentation associated with the software and platform version you are using.

The Arm Morello platform is a research and prototyping system designed to enable software development, porting, and evaluation of CHERI-based architectures. However, it is not representative of a production-quality CHERI implementation and should therefore not be used as the sole basis for assessing the performance overhead of CHERI.

Performance results obtained on Morello may reflect characteristics of the prototype hardware, development-stage toolchains, and implementation choices specific to the research platform, rather than the intrinsic cost of CHERI itself. Consequently, direct comparisons between Morello and conventional production processors can lead to misleading conclusions regarding CHERI performance overhead.

We recommend using Morello primarily for software development, compatibility testing, and functional evaluation. Once an application has been ported and validated, researchers should seek to corroborate performance results using additional CHERI platforms, implementations, simulators, or published results that better reflect production-oriented designs. Real-world workload measurements across multiple platforms provide a more reliable basis for understanding the true performance impact of CHERI. The CHERI Alliance can provide guidance on available platforms and benchmarking opportunities to support such evaluations.
Use the Arm Morello resources, CheriBSD Getting Started, and cheribuild for current technical instructions. For its place in the wider timeline, read Morello History.

Simulation is the quickest way to build a first CHERIoT application, but embedded development soon needs physical input and output. Developers must test timers, UARTs, storage, sensors, displays, and fault behaviour on hardware.
Sonata provides a purpose-built FPGA platform for that stage.

Developed by lowRISC, Sonata combines an FPGA implementation of a CHERIoT-capable system with a board and peripherals intended for embedded prototyping. It gives software developers a more direct route than assembling a processor core, system-on-chip design, and generic FPGA board themselves.

The platform is open and works with the CHERIoT real-time operating system (RTOS), software development kit (SDK), examples, and build flow. The CHERIoT project also provides a Sonata simulation route, allowing software to move between simulated and physical versions of a closely related platform.
The exact board identifiers and deployment scripts follow the current RTOS and Sonata releases. Use the maintained documentation rather than an older copied command.
Its physical interfaces let developers test the parts that an instruction-set simulator cannot represent realistically.

Repeat timing-sensitive and hardware-integration tests on the board. Simulation speed is not a processor performance measurement.
Visit the Sonata project documentation and the CHERIoT getting-started guide for current hardware and software instructions.

The X730 is a commercially licensable 64-bit application-processor core implementing CHERI-RISC-V. The baseline design is described as an in-order, dual-issue, nine-stage processor with a memory-management unit, extended to handle capabilities and CHERI instructions.
The X730 is an RVA22 compliant processor with the following optional/extra extensions.

Verification of X730 has been extensive. It has followed a strategy of deconstructing the design into its constituent components and major subsystems, then verifying those independently. This has been done with a mixture of formal property-based environments and simulation, and resulted in ~17 different verification environments, including:

These separate environments allow the verification of each component to explore corner cases far easier than if they were only tested when integrated into the full design. The layering of verification environments (like the CHERI formal and the full execution pipeline above) allows the detection and tracking of "escapes" from one layer to the next. These then drive the improvement of the verification.

All verification results are tracked against requirements to ensure that everything that has been specified has been covered by at least one of the environments and gaps do not form between environments. Codasip's processes have been reviewed by TUV/SUD and 32-bit configurations generated from the same code-base has received ISO 26262 certification for use in automotive applications.
In total, over 40 person-years of engineering effort has been put into X730's verification.
In hybrid/integer mode: PCC and DDC are implicitly added to integer pointers.
Page table walks are not bounded by capabilities.

Capabilities are checked within their own virtual address space. The software that manages the address space is bound by capabilities (within its address space) but may abuse address translation to allow lesser privileged code to breach its isolation. Thus these software elements must form part of the trusted code base of the system.

Debug mode disables all CHERI checks. Debug mode is not expected to be active in normal operation. Debug mode can only be entered via RISC-V standard methods. SoC-level security controls are expected on the external debug interface.

X730 only transforms tagged capabilities according to the proposed RVY extension, which does not allow any tagged values to be written to a register that are not derived from capabilities with equal or greater privilege. In addition, only aligned, capability-wide writes and reads preserve the tag from the register, and all other writes clear the capability tag. There are therefore no instructions that can set a tag on arbitrary values in a register or overwrite a tagged value in memory with an arbitrary value without clearing the tag.
Beyond the scope of this certification, we have carefully engineered the memory subsystems to ensure that the commitment to memory of capabilities preserves atomicity with their tags.

Our CPU core has a single bus master for data accesses and so cannot make concurrent writes. When in a multi-core configuration the cores cannot make concurrent writes to the same cache line due to the coherent memory system. Cores can make concurrent writes to the same uncached memory address, and these are ordered by the L2 cache before being sent to the SoC memory system. The L2 cache treats the capabilities as atomic units that cannot be partially overwritten. The L2 cache, by its nature, cannot make concurrent accesses to the system memories.

The X730 implements RV64Y Svyrg, which enables temporal safety for allocated memory in virtual address spaces: a supervisor can entirely remove access to freed virtual addresses before the memory is reallocated by placing freed memory regions in quarantine and using a background sweeper thread to find any dangling references before reallocation.

CHERI uses a combination of hardware and software to implement temporal safety on the MMU-based X730 core. CHERI allows temporal safety to be enforced by making it possible to accurately identify pointers, and check the memory which they are permitted to access. There have been various papers published on this topic (CHERIvoke, Cornucopia and Cornucopia Reloaded). Each offers improved performance over the previous paper. The X730 implements a 4-bit PTE scheme to accelerate revocation using the scheme from Cornucopia Reloaded allowing virtual memory pages to have their capabilities accurately tracked. It provides Capability Dirty Tracking to identify which pages have had capabilities stored to them, and a load barrier to prevent capabilities from being loaded from pages which have not yet been swept for stale capabilities which would allow use-after-reallocation vulnerabilities. Freed memory regions are held in quarantine until all stale capabilities which refer to them have been swept (located and invalidated).

Linux is at the heart of many products, platforms and services. CHERI Linux is the effort to extend CHERI support through the Linux software stack, allowing existing Linux environments to take advantage of capability-based memory protection.

Supporting CHERI involves more than enabling a processor and compiler. Capabilities must work correctly through the kernel, virtual memory, system calls, executable loading, libraries, debugging and the wider user-space environment.
For organisations already building products and services around Linux, CHERI Linux provides a route towards adopting CHERI while retaining the familiar Linux ecosystem.
It is particularly relevant when you want to:
CHERI support reaches across the Linux software stack. Areas of development include:

Kernel support and pure-capability user space are closely related, but they are distinct areas of development. A kernel capable of running on CHERI hardware does not by itself provide a complete pure-capability Linux environment.
A CHERI Linux development environment can bring together:
The exact environment depends on the processor architecture and implementation. Processor suppliers may also provide an integrated SDK containing compatible versions of these components.
CHERI Linux development includes work targeting CHERI-RISC-V, alongside experience gained from earlier Linux development for Morello.
Support varies between processor implementations and software configurations, so developers should use the kernel, toolchain, libraries and platform software recommended for their chosen target.

A minimal Linux system that boots on a CHERI processor and a broad pure-capability Linux environment are also different milestones. Application, library, package and driver coverage grows as more of the ecosystem is adapted and tested.
Ultimately, CHERI Linux is about more than booting Linux on CHERI hardware.
For CHERI protection to extend through real workloads, capabilities need to be supported consistently across the operating system, system libraries, application interfaces and software packages.

This makes CHERI Linux relevant to both kernel and platform developers, who are enabling the underlying architecture, and application developers, who want to build and port software for CHERI-enabled Linux systems.

CHERI Linux is a cross-project effort rather than a single processor-specific port. The CHERI Alliance Linux Working Group brings organisations and developers together to coordinate priorities, share implementation experience and help drive convergence across CHERI architectures and platforms.
The longer-term goal is to reduce platform-specific fragmentation and establish common approaches that can support CHERI integration across the wider Linux ecosystem.
Choose CHERI Linux when Linux APIs, drivers, applications or deployment environments are important to your target system.
Other CHERI operating-system environments serve complementary needs. For example:
CHERI Linux is therefore particularly important for bringing CHERI into the large body of software and products already built around Linux.

CHERI Zephyr brings capability-based memory protection to the Zephyr ecosystem, providing a route for developers who want to explore CHERI while retaining familiar Zephyr APIs, drivers, build tools and development practices.

Supporting CHERI involves more than enabling a processor and compiler. Capability protection also needs to work across the operating system, including threads, memory, interrupts, drivers and interactions between application and kernel code.

Zephyr is already used as the software foundation for many embedded systems. CHERI-enabled Zephyr explores how these existing software environments can benefit from hardware-enforced memory protection without adopting an entirely different operating-system model.
It is particularly relevant when you want to:
CHERI protection extends beyond the processor into parts of the operating system that create, store or use pointers and capabilities.
Together, these changes allow Zephyr software to make use of CHERI's hardware-enforced memory protection.
CHERI Zephyr development brings together the CHERI processor architecture, compiler and toolchain, Zephyr kernel, board configurations, drivers, samples and tests.

Support is progressing at different pace depending on architectures, processors, boards, drivers and Zephyr configurations, so developers should use the software and platform combination recommended for their chosen CHERI target.
As support develops, the goal is not simply to boot Zephyr on a CHERI processor, but to extend meaningful capability protection through applications and the wider operating-system environment.
Both CHERI-enabled Zephyr and CHERIoT address embedded systems, but they provide different routes to adopting CHERI.

The choice is therefore not simply about which platform is more mature. It depends on whether your priority is bringing CHERI to an existing embedded software ecosystem or adopting a platform designed around CHERI from the outset.
The CHERI Alliance Zephyr Working Group coordinates collaboration around CHERI Zephyr, bringing together implementation work, platform support, testing and contributions.
A key objective is to reduce fragmentation between individual CHERI implementations and build common approaches that can support CHERI across the broader Zephyr ecosystem.
CHERI Zephyr is particularly useful when you want to:
For projects that instead want an embedded hardware and software platform designed around capability-based compartmentalisation from the outset, CHERIoT provides a complementary route.
CheriBSD extends FreeBSD with support for CHERI, providing a complete application-class environment for developing, porting and testing CHERI software on CHERI-RISC-V and Arm Morello.
It brings CHERI capabilities through the operating system and software stack, allowing developers to work with real applications, libraries and services rather than isolated examples.

CheriBSD provides a familiar Unix environment in which developers can explore how existing software behaves when pointers become CHERI capabilities and hardware-enforced memory protection extends across applications and the operating system.
For many developers exploring application-class CHERI, CheriBSD provides the software environment in which the different parts of the CHERI ecosystem come together.
CheriBSD supports both hybrid and pure-capability software models.
In a hybrid environment, conventional pointers and CHERI capabilities can coexist, providing a route for progressively adapting existing software.
In a pure-capability environment, language-visible pointers are represented as capabilities, allowing CHERI protection to be applied systematically throughout applications and supporting libraries.

CheriBSD's pure-capability environment, known as CheriABI, has enabled substantial existing software to be ported and tested, providing valuable experience of the compatibility issues that arise when moving existing code to capability-based systems.
CHERI support in a general-purpose operating system goes far beyond the processor and compiler. Capabilities need to work throughout the software stack.
CheriBSD integrates CHERI across areas including:
This provides a complete environment for exploring CHERI at application and system level.
cheribuild provides an integrated route for building a compatible CHERI toolchain, QEMU, CheriBSD and disk image.

This allows developers to create a complete application-class CHERI development environment without requiring physical hardware, making it a practical starting point for software development and porting.
CheriBSD supports Morello's hybrid and pure-capability software environments.
Together with the corresponding CHERI compiler, firmware and platform support, Morello provides a physical application-class platform for developing and evaluating CHERI software.
CheriBSD can also run on supported CHERI-RISC-V processor and FPGA platforms where the architecture and system implementation provide the required operating-system support.
Support is platform-specific, so check the processor architecture, CheriBSD version and board configuration before selecting a hardware target.
One of CheriBSD's most important roles has been providing a realistic environment for understanding how existing software adapts to CHERI.
Many applications compile with relatively small changes, while others expose assumptions about:
These are often exactly the assumptions that need attention when moving existing software towards a pure-capability environment.

CheriBSD extends FreeBSD rather than defining a completely separate operating system. It retains familiar Unix interfaces, networking, filesystems, build infrastructure and source organisation while adding the architectural and software changes needed for CHERI.
Generally useful changes can be contributed to FreeBSD, while CHERI-specific architecture and ABI development can continue within CheriBSD.
A standard FreeBSD installation should therefore not be confused with a complete CheriBSD environment.
CheriBSD is particularly useful when you want to:

CheriBSD is primarily a research and development platform for application-class CHERI, rather than a direct replacement for Linux or a single fixed product configuration. Its extensive integration of CHERI across the kernel, ABI, libraries and user space also makes it a useful reference for operating-system developers implementing CHERI support elsewhere.
For developers getting started, the natural route is cheribuild + QEMU + CheriBSD, before moving to an FPGA or physical CHERI platform when hardware-specific behaviour becomes important.

CHERI adds information to pointers, including bounds, permissions and protected validity information. Capability-aware debugging tools make this state visible alongside familiar addresses, registers, variables, symbols and stack traces.
When CHERI prevents an invalid memory access, these tools can help developers understand what the program tried to do, which capability it used, and why the operation was rejected.
A CHERI capability fault occurs when software attempts an operation that is not permitted by the capability it is using.
Depending on the platform and tools, diagnostics may show information such as:
This can make CHERI faults valuable during development: rather than allowing an invalid access to silently corrupt memory, the hardware can stop it at the point where protection is violated.
The exact diagnostics and terminology vary between CHERI platforms.
Capability-aware versions of GDB and LLDB extend familiar debugging workflows with support for CHERI capabilities.
Alongside source code, breakpoints, registers, memory and stack traces, supported debugger builds can expose capability registers and their associated bounds, permissions and state.
Debugger support depends on the target architecture, ABI and platform, so use the debugger supplied or recommended for your CHERI development environment.
QEMU provides a convenient environment for investigating capability faults without requiring physical hardware.
Because QEMU provides an architectural rather than physical implementation model, hardware-specific behaviour may require an FPGA or silicon platform.
Different CHERI software environments integrate capability debugging in different ways.
Debugging sometimes starts before the program runs. CHERI-aware binary tools can help developers inspect how capabilities are represented in compiled software.

Tools such as llvm-readelf, llvm-objdump, and nm can be used, with appropriate CHERI support, to examine areas such as symbols, sections, relocations, generated instructions and capability-related information in executable files.
These tools can be particularly useful when investigating compiler, linker, loader or ABI issues.

Capability-aware debugging is currently closely tied to the underlying CHERI architecture, ABI, operating system and software environment. A conventional debugger may be able to display the raw contents of a capability-sized value without understanding all of its CHERI-specific state.
CHERI changes an important part of the debugging experience: memory errors that might otherwise cause corruption or appear much later can instead become explicit capability faults.

Capability-aware diagnostics help developers trace those faults back to incorrect pointer use, insufficient authority or other software assumptions, making debugging tools an important part of the CHERI development environment.

LLVM and Clang provide the compiler foundation for much of the CHERI software ecosystem. They translate ordinary language-level operations, such as accessing objects through pointers, into code that uses CHERI capabilities and the protection they provide.
Clang is the C and C++ compiler developers interact with, while LLVM provides the underlying compiler infrastructure and code generation.

CHERI hardware uses capabilities to control how software accesses memory. The compiler plays an important role in creating and preserving those capabilities as it translates source code into machine code.
Depending on the target platform, Clang can support:

In many cases, existing C and C++ software can be compiled for CHERI with relatively small changes, while code that makes assumptions about pointers, memory layouts or integer conversions may require more attention.
CHERI platforms can support different ways of introducing capabilities into existing software.
In a hybrid environment, conventional pointers can coexist with CHERI capabilities. This can be useful when bringing up platforms and progressively adapting existing software.
In a pure-capability environment, pointers are represented as CHERI capabilities throughout applications and supporting software, providing stronger and more systematic enforcement.

The available models and ABIs depend on the target platform. Morello, application-class CHERI-RISC-V and CHERIoT therefore use toolchains configured for their respective architectures and software environments.

The cheribuild environment brings together a compatible LLVM and Clang toolchain, system headers, linker, QEMU, and CheriBSD image. It supports application-class CHERI-RISC-V work across hybrid and pure-capability software configurations.
Morello uses an Arm-based CHERI compiler and ABI together with its corresponding system software and platform support.
The Morello software environment has been widely used to develop and port applications to CHERI and explore the transition between conventional and pure-capability software.
The CHERIoT SDK uses a Clang-based toolchain aligned with the CHERIoT instruction set, RTOS, compartment model, linker, and firmware build system.

Parts of CHERI support are already present in upstream LLVM, while complete target support can still depend on platform-specific branches and releases. A key focus for the CHERI Alliance is bringing this work together, driving convergence across CHERI platforms and helping move towards common, upstream LLVM support.
CHERI compilers can use information about objects and allocations to create capabilities with appropriate bounds and permissions.

How tightly those bounds are applied can vary between platforms and configurations, balancing stronger protection with compatibility requirements. As a result, compiler version, target architecture, ABI and software environment all matter when building or comparing CHERI software.

Code that assumes that pointers and integers have the same representation, or relies heavily on particular object layouts or pointer manipulation, may need additional attention when moving to a CHERI target.
For most developers, there is no need to build or understand the CHERI compiler infrastructure itself. Start with the toolchain supplied or recommended for your chosen platform.

For application-class CHERI development, cheribuild provides an integrated route to LLVM/Clang, QEMU and CheriBSD. For embedded development, use the toolchain and SDK associated with the target platform, such as CHERIoT.
From there, the next step is to compile existing software, understand any compatibility warnings or errors, and progressively adapt the code to make effective use of CHERI's protection.

CHERI porting is not one centrally versioned programme. It spans processor architectures, compilers, operating systems, real-time environments, runtimes, applications, packages, emulators, and hardware platforms maintained by different projects.

A project can support capability instructions without providing a pure-capability application ABI. An operating system can boot before it has broad driver or package coverage. A library can compile while still depending on untested pointer assumptions. These are different forms of progress rather than steps on one universal scale.
Status claims also change with architecture revisions, toolchain branches, kernel versions, board support, and release processes.

The most current information lives with the project that owns a branch, release, SDK, board configuration, package set, or test environment. Alliance Working Groups connect several of these projects and publish roadmaps, repositories, articles, and event updates where shared coordination is useful.
This page describes the structure of that landscape. Individual platform and software pages link to the corresponding public project records.

Embedded systems cover a wide range of timing, memory, power, assurance, device, and compatibility requirements. CHERI appears in this landscape through both new capability-oriented platforms and ports of established real-time operating systems.

CHERIoT co-designs a CHERI instruction-set profile, RTOS, compartment model, linker, allocator, and SDK for small embedded systems. Capability protection is part of the platform's foundation rather than an extension to a conventional process model.

CHERI-Zephyr brings capability state and memory protection into Zephyr's existing kernel, APIs, drivers, configuration system, and board ecosystem. Its attraction is continuity with software already built around Zephyr.

CHERI FreeRTOS work explores capability protection and compartments around a widely deployed real-time kernel and its familiar application interfaces. The Alliance working group provides a forum for common approaches across ports and platforms.

seL4 is a verified microkernel rather than a conventional RTOS, but it is relevant to embedded and real-time systems that need strong isolation and assurance. CHERI work connects architectural memory capabilities with seL4's existing capability-based kernel model and Microkit components.

The projects differ in architecture profile, kernel model, compartment design, existing APIs, device support, toolchain integration, temporal-safety mechanisms, assurance evidence, and relationship with upstream communities.
Those differences reflect distinct product and research goals. They are not interchangeable implementations of one CHERI RTOS specification.
Related groups include CHERI FreeRTOS, CHERI Zephyr, CHERI for seL4, and MMU-less Systems.

Rust and CHERI provide complementary approaches to memory safety. Rust provides language-level protections, while CHERI adds hardware-enforced protection at run time, including around unsafe code, native interfaces and compartment boundaries.
For a broader explanation of how the two technologies complement each other, see the CHERI and Rust technical overview.

Supporting Rust on a CHERI platform involves more than adding a compiler target. The compiler, pointer representation, application binary interface (ABI), libraries, allocator, operating-system interfaces, native bindings, debugger and build tools all need to work with CHERI capabilities.

In particular, CHERI capability pointers may differ from conventional pointers in size and representation. Code that makes assumptions about pointer sizes, integer conversions or data layouts may therefore need attention.
Safe Rust prevents many memory-safety errors before software runs, but real systems may also contain unsafe Rust, native libraries, operating-system components or code written in other languages.

On a CHERI platform, hardware capabilities can constrain the memory and permissions available to this code, providing an additional layer of protection where Rust's language-level guarantees do not apply.
CHERI does not make unsafe Rust automatically safe, or replace Rust's rules around aliasing, lifetimes and initialisation. Instead, the two provide complementary protection at different layers.
Rust applications often need to interact with existing C or C++ libraries, operating-system services and other native components through foreign-function interfaces (FFIs).
On CHERI platforms, these interfaces also need to account for capability pointers, including their bounds and permissions, as well as ABI, memory-allocation, object-layout and ownership requirements.
This makes mixed-language interfaces an important area to test when bringing existing Rust software to CHERI.
Rust work for Morello has included freestanding and CheriBSD environments, compiler targets, libraries and native interfaces.
These environments provide a route for exploring Rust on an application-class CHERI platform. Particular configurations may depend on project-specific toolchains and versions.
Rust support is also being developed for CHERI-RISC-V, including pure-capability environments and operating-system integration.
Available compiler targets, libraries, package support and operating-system environments vary between projects and implementations.
Rust support is developing within the CHERIoT embedded ecosystem.
The established CHERIoT development environment is centred on its C and C++ SDK, while Rust work is extending support across the compiler, runtime and compartment interfaces.
Rust support is not yet uniform across all CHERI platforms. Before starting development, check:
Pinning the toolchain and platform versions used by a project can also help keep builds and tests reproducible.
Rust support across CHERI is continuing to evolve across compiler, operating-system, embedded and hardware projects.
The Rust + CHERI Working Group connects this work across the CHERI Alliance and aims for convergence and compatibility. CHERI and Rust provides the broader architectural context.
Simulation is often the easiest way to get started with CHERI. It lets you develop, port and test software before you have access to CHERI hardware.

Different simulators serve different purposes. Some run complete operating systems and applications relatively quickly, while others provide detailed models of the CHERI architecture or a particular processor implementation.
For most software developers, QEMU is a good place to start. It can run complete CHERI software environments and is well suited to application development, porting and automated testing.
For architecture and hardware developers, more detailed models are available:
The right choice depends on what you want to learn.

CHERI-enabled QEMU provides a convenient way to run complete CHERI software environments without physical hardware. cheribuild can build QEMU together with matching development tools, operating systems and disk images.

QEMU models architectural behaviour rather than a particular processor's physical implementation. It should therefore not be used to predict processor performance or hardware characteristics such as detailed cache, speculation or timing behaviour.
Sail is a formal model that provides executable descriptions of instruction-set behaviour and is used in CHERI architecture development, reference simulation, test generation and formal reasoning.
It is particularly useful when the question is "What should this CHERI instruction do?" rather than "How quickly will this software run?"
Sail models can also provide an independent reference against which processor implementations can be compared.
When using an executable architecture model, make sure its CHERI instruction-set architecture (ISA) version matches the system or implementation you are testing.
The CHERIoT development environment provides simulation routes for both architecture and processor-implementation models.
This allows developers to run compartmentalised firmware in simulation before moving to an FPGA or production hardware, and to test software at different levels of abstraction during development.
Register-transfer-level (RTL) simulation runs the processor's actual hardware description and is primarily useful to processor and hardware developers.

RTL simulation provides much more implementation detail than QEMU, but is significantly slower. It is therefore generally better suited to focused hardware tests and smaller software workloads than running complete applications and operating systems.
Compiled implementation models, using tools such as Verilator, can provide another route for running some hardware designs more quickly while retaining implementation-specific behaviour.

Whichever route you choose, check that the simulator, CHERI ISA version, compiler and software environment are compatible.
Simulation lets you start developing with CHERI without waiting for physical hardware.
Use Run CHERI in Simulation for a first practical setup, and move to FPGA Platforms when the question depends on hardware implementation.
The Certification Program Working Group is responsible for defining the CHERI Enabled program for CHERI products:

The group aims to continuously improve the certification program. This involves regularly reviewing and updating the guidelines, processes, and systems to enhance efficiency, effectiveness, and relevance

Overall, the working group plays a crucial role in ensuring the compliance and compatibility of certified CHERI products to make sure that users can trust the CHERI logo to guarantee a correct implementation of the technology.

CHERI provides memory safety for C-like languages. Every CHERI implementation will trap on buffer overflows in C and many will trap on use-after-free. Beyond that, C compilers provide builtins for CHERI-specific and CHERI-implementation-specific features, additional headers, and so on.

The security properties of a CHERI system depend on how software is built, compiled, structured, and compartmentalised. Two products may both claim to "use CHERI" while providing very different levels of protection.
To understand what protection a system actually provides, engineers should ask a few practical questions about architecture, authority, threat models, and evidence.
Before discussing CHERI features, identify the data, services, and operations that matter:
CHERI can only enforce security boundaries that exist in the software architecture. If every component has access to everything, there is little isolation for the hardware to enforce.
Security depends on what you expect the system to defend against. A browser renderer, a cloud service, and an industrial controller will have very different threat models.

Different CHERI deployments provide different security properties. Verify which protections are enabled in your system rather than assuming they come automatically from CHERI hardware.

Most well-structured C and C++ code does not need a redesign for CHERI. The difficult parts are usually places where a program has hidden the difference between an address, a pointer, an object boundary, and an authority decision.
A good port makes those assumptions visible and fixes their root cause. Suppressing the warning or widening every bound may restore execution while discarding the security benefit.
Start with a small leaf library or command-line component. A narrow target makes compiler diagnostics and runtime faults easier to understand.
Code sometimes stores a pointer in an integer, modifies its low bits, or serialises it directly:

On CHERI, an address alone does not contain the capability's bounds, permissions, provenance, or tag. Use pointer types for pointers. Where the platform supports a documented address conversion, use uintptr_t and keep the original capability needed to derive valid authority.
Converting an integer back to a pointer does not, by itself, create a valid capability.
Pure-capability pointers may be larger than conventional pointers. Review:
Store an index, offset, or validated protocol identifier in a persistent or wire format rather than a live in-memory pointer.
CHERI may expose code that deliberately walks from one object into another, derives a container pointer from a member, or expects an allocator to return wider storage than requested.

Decide what the object really is. If several fields form one allocation, retain a capability for the enclosing allocation and derive bounded field capabilities from it. Avoid solving every fault by granting access to the whole address space.

An allocator must return capabilities with useful bounds and preserve tags when storing metadata. It may also participate in temporal-safety mechanisms. Prefer the platform allocator first, then port a custom allocator using the architecture and operating-system guidance.

Capabilities have protected tags outside the ordinary byte representation. Byte copies through supported memory operations can preserve tagged values when alignment and size requirements are met, but writing arbitrary bytes cannot forge a tag.

Review custom memcpy, compression, encryption, shared-memory, and device-transfer code. A capability is meaningful only within a suitable address-space and authority context, so it should not be treated as portable serialised data.

Inline assembly must use the correct capability registers, constraints, calling convention, and clobber list. Isolate it behind a small, tested interface. Prefer compiler intrinsics or maintained platform code where available.
Keep this log with the port. It helps reviewers distinguish compatibility changes from changes that alter the security model.
